entities.summary:
Aleatoric music, emerging prominently in the 20th century, represents a radical shift in the creative process of musical composition and performance. Pioneered by influential composers such as John Cage and Karlheinz Stockhausen, this genre deliberately incorporates elements of chance, inviting unpredictability and spontaneity into the musical experience. Originating in Europe and quickly gaining traction globally, the movement reflects broader 20th-century artistic trends that sought to challenge traditional norms and embrace innovative forms of expression. Aleatoric music matters not only as a genre but also as a reflection of a cultural zeitgeist that questioned established paradigms across the arts.

The development of aleatoric music can be traced back to Cage's groundbreaking work in the 1950s, particularly his composition '4'33'', which consists of periods of silence, emphasizing the sounds of the environment. This work, along with Stockhausen's 'Klavierstück XI', which allows performers to choose the order of their parts, exemplifies the shift towards an interactive relationship between composer and performer. Such compositions were radical for their time, as they dismantled the rigid structures of classical music and encouraged audiences to engage in active listening. The movement gained momentum in various cultural hubs, from New York to Darmstadt, influencing a wide range of musical styles and leading to the emergence of other experimental practices.
